note: WHICH AUTHORITY KEPT PRAIRIE AVENUE IN 1904: THE CITY. The 1911 Sanborn sheets print 'Prairie Av. Blvd.' and 'E. 16th St. (Boulevard)', and the question T-1728 was asked is which body paved and kept a boulevard in 1904. The answer this compilation gives is that Prairie Avenue was not yet one. The city's consent to the South Park Commissioners taking 'Prairie avenue, from the north line of Sixteenth street to the south line of Twenty-ninth street' and Sixteenth Street from Michigan to Prairie 'for park and boulevard purposes, in order to connect Michigan boulevard ... with the South Park' was passed 30 October 1905 (p. 119), and the Commissioners' own ordinance selecting and taking them, reciting frontage consents from a majority of the owners, was passed 24 October 1906 (pp. 123-125), after which 'full power and authority to regulate, control, improve, and maintain' them vested in the Commissioners, the city keeping its water, gas and sewer rights. An earlier consent of 28 May 1904 (chicago_council_proceedings_1904_v53) did not produce a taking; this compilation prints only the 1905 ordinance. The Commissioners' municipal code of 1897 (archive.org/details/municipalcodeofs00chic, also read) lists no Prairie Avenue boulevard.
what_it_supplies: the dates on which Prairie Avenue 16th-29th and E. 16th Street (Michigan to Prairie) became South Park boulevards: city consent 30 October 1905, taking 24 October 1906
hence that on 1 July 1904 both were city streets, paved by the Board of Local Improvements and repaired by the Department of Public Works
what_it_does_not_supply: any surface, width or planting the Commissioners gave the avenue after 1906
